summary: Defines a mechanism for domain owners to tell DNS clients about local resolvers that are authorized to answer for certain names in split-horizon deployments. Clients that do not use that resolver by default can then use it just for those names.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a building has its own phone book for its own names. This lets the owner of a name vouch for that phone book so your device trusts it.

questions: how to trust a local dns resolver for a domain
how does a client validate a local dns resolver
subtitle: How a domain owner can vouch for a network's local DNS resolver, so clients use it only for the names it is allowed to answer.

tldr.problem: Networks can hint that certain domains get special local treatment, but a client cannot tell whether the domain owner actually authorized that.
tldr.mechanism: The network sends the client an authorization claim naming a local encrypted resolver and the subdomains it serves. The parent zone publishes a TXT Verification Record containing a hashed token, and the client checks that record over a tamperproof resolution path.
tldr.outcome: A client can safely send queries for just the validated subdomains to the local resolver, with no prior configuration, while using another resolution method for everything else.

facts.label: Verification Record type
facts.value: TXT at ADN, then _splitdns-challenge, then parent zone

today: RFC 9704 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2025, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is therefore the current definition of validated split-horizon DNS authority.

sections.title: The Split-Horizon Problem
sections.content:
In split-horizon DNS, a network's resolver acts as an authoritative server for some names and gives different answers from inside the network than the global DNS does. Networks usually offer a resolver through DHCP or IPv6 Router Advertisements. Clients that send all queries to it always get the split-horizon answers, and clients that never use it never do. Those two kinds of client are out of scope.

This RFC targets hybrid clients. Several existing mechanisms give clients 'local domain hints', such as PvD dnsZones and IKEv2 INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN, but none lets a client check that the domain owner authorized the special treatment. Clients must decide for themselves whether to trust the hint.

RFC 9704 lets the network establish its authority to the client, and lets the client confirm that the domain owner approved it. This needs cooperation between the local DNS zone and the public zone.
sections.eli5: A building can claim 'ask our front desk about our own rooms'. But how do you know the owner of those rooms agreed? This RFC is the way to check.

sections.title: Scope and Requirements
sections.content:
The protocol supports a domain owner creating or authorizing a split-horizon view of their own domain. It does not support split-horizon views created by anyone else, so DNS filtering is not enabled by it. It applies to any network offering split-horizon DNS, and the endpoint needs no prior configuration. Special-Use Domain Names such as home.arpa. and local. MUST NOT be validated this way, and the specification is limited to DNS servers that support authenticated encryption and names rooted in the global DNS.

The design aims for five properties: no loss of security, least privilege (local resolvers hold no secrets that could weaken the public zone), local zone confidentiality, flexibility in representing split zone structures, and DNSSEC compatibility.
sections.eli5: It is only for owners vouching for their own names, and it is built so that a mistake in the local phone book cannot put the real one at risk.

sections.title: Authorization Claims and Verification Records
sections.content:
A participating network MUST offer one or more encrypted resolvers through DNR or DDR options, or an equivalent. It MUST then convey one or more authorization claims. Each claim contains: the Authentication Domain Name (ADN) of a local encrypted resolver, the name of the authorizing parent zone, the set of claimed subdomains (an asterisk alone claims the whole parent zone), a ZONEMD hash algorithm, and a high-entropy salt of up to 255 octets.

The network gives the claim to the parent zone operator. If approved, the operator computes a Verification Token: sort the subdomains in canonical order, replace the parent suffix with a zero octet, concatenate the results as $X, and compute the hash of the salt length, the salt and $X joined together. The operator publishes a TXT record at the ADN, then _splitdns-challenge, then the parent zone name, with contents such as token=base64url($TOKEN). Publishing it authorizes the resolver to serve those subdomains.

Claims reach the client in one of two encodings. In DHCP, a claim is an Authentication option using Protocol value 4, 'Split-horizon DNS', with the Replay Detection Method set to 0x00. With Provisioning Domains, the PvD Additional Information key splitDnsClaims holds a JSON array of objects with resolver, parent, subdomains, algorithm and salt.
sections.eli5: The owner stamps a secret code on a public notice board saying 'this front desk may answer for these rooms'. The code can only be made by someone who knows the claim.

sections.title: Validating the Claim
sections.content:
To validate, the client MUST resolve the Verification Record. If the result contains the expected token, the client SHALL regard the named resolver as authoritative for the claimed subdomains. Each validation applies only to one ADN. A zone becomes a Validated Split-Horizon zone after successful validation by a 'tamperproof' resolution method, one the local network operator cannot interfere with. Two are given.

  • Preconfigured external resolver: if the client already sends queries to a resolver outside the network over an encrypted transport, that path is treated as tamperproof. If no answer arrives in a reasonable time, verification fails. The client MUST NOT relax its usual acceptance rules for this query.
  • DNSSEC: the client resolves the record by any method and performs full DNSSEC validation locally. A Secure result is used; Bogus or Indeterminate results are rejected; for Insecure the client SHOULD retry by another method, and if it does not, it MUST treat validation as failed.

Verification Records expire with their TTL or signature validity, and clients MUST fetch them again shortly before expiry. Section 11 also describes updating a claim by DHCP reconfiguration or by incrementing the sequence number in the RA PvD Option. The old record must be kept until the DHCP lease or PvD information expires, and the salt MUST be regenerated whenever a claim is updated.
sections.eli5: Your device checks the notice board in a way the building cannot tamper with, either by asking a faraway helper or by checking a signature seal.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, the client learns the network's DNS server (dns.example.net) and PvD ID (pvd.example.com) through DNR, connects with an encrypted transport, and fetches the PvD Additional Information over HTTPS. That JSON carries a splitDnsClaims entry claiming the whole parent, written as an asterisk, under parent example.com with algorithm SHA384.

With an external resolver, the client sends a TXT query for dns.example.net._splitdns-challenge.example.com and compares the returned token with the claim. With DNSSEC, it sends the same query with the DO bit to the network's resolver and checks the RRSIG. If the token matches, the client sends queries for names within the claimed zones to the local resolver.

For efficiency, the RFC recommends keeping internal names in a child zone (for example internal.example.com) of the advertised hint, which reduces how often the Verification Record has to change.
sections.eli5: The device learns who runs the front desk, reads the owner's code from the public board, and if the code matches, it asks the front desk about those rooms.

sections.title: DNSSEC Delegation and Security Notes
sections.content:
If the local zone can be signed with globally trusted keys for the parent zone, DNSSEC works through an ordinary zone cut with a DS record. To avoid giving the local resolver the parent's private keys, the parent MAY add a ds=... key to the Verification Record, holding the base64url RDATA of a DS record. It authorizes a DNSKEY whose owner name is resolver.arpa.. The client MAY then query that DNSKEY from the local resolver, at least one result MUST match the DS, and all local results for the claim MUST chain to an approved DNSKEY. Without a globally trusted DNSKEY, claimed subdomains MUST be marked unsigned in the public DNS.

On security: the ADNs of authorized resolvers appear in Verification Record owner names, which can leak sensitive names, so resolvers should be named without revealing anything sensitive. Hash algorithm agility comes from the ZONEMD Hash Algorithms registry, and the salt depends on a high-quality random number generator.
sections.eli5: The owner can hand over a one-way check for the front desk's signature without ever giving the desk the owner's own pen.
